scenes.line: The photo sequence shows the squid homing in on the baited line and enveloping it in a ball of tentacles. The researchers were able to locate the likely general location of giant squid by closely tailing the movements of sperm whales.
scenes.image_prompt: A detailed underwater still image showing entangled marine forms in dark water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Journal publication
scenes.line: Kubodera and Mori reported their observations in the journal Proceedings of the Royal Society. Among other things, the observations demonstrate actual hunting behaviors of adult Architeuthis.
scenes.image_prompt: A stack of academic scientific journals resting on a wooden table., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Aggressive feeding technique
scenes.line: The observations suggest that the species has a much more aggressive feeding technique. In November 2006, American explorer and diver Scott Cassell led an expedition to the Gulf of California.
scenes.image_prompt: Underwater view of dark pelagic water fading into blackness., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Humboldt squid camera method
scenes.line: The team employed a novel filming method using a Humboldt squid carrying a specially designed camera clipped to its fin. The footage aired a year later on a History Channel program, MonsterQuest: Giant Squid Found.
scenes.image_prompt: A marine camera housing attached with heavy duty straps., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: NHK and Discovery expedition
scenes.line: In July 2012, a crew from television networks NHK and Discovery Channel captured footage using submersibles. To capture the footage the team aboard OceanX's vessel MV Alucia traveled to the Ogasawara Islands and utilized submersibles.
scenes.image_prompt: A modern marine research vessel equipped with an A-frame crane on deck., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Bioluminescence luring technique
scenes.line: The squid was drawn into viewing range by artificial bioluminescence created to mimic panicking Atolla jellyfish. The giant squid was filmed feeding for about 23 minutes by Tsunemi Kubodera until it departed.
scenes.image_prompt: Glowing blue bioluminescent organisms floating in dark deep sea water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

long_what_powers_the_bizarre_ecosystems_.title: What Powers the Bizarre Ecosystems of Hydrothermal Vents Rising From the Deep Ocean Floor?

scenes.label: Fissures on seabed
scenes.line: Hydrothermal vents are fissures on the seabed from which geothermally heated water discharges. They are commonly found near volcanically active places, areas where tectonic plates are moving apart at mid-ocean ridges, ocean basins, and hotspots.
scenes.image_prompt: Fissures on the dark seabed emitting heated water into the deep ocean., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Hydrothermal plumes
scenes.line: The dispersal of hydrothermal fluids throughout the global ocean at active vent sites creates hydrothermal plumes. Hydrothermal deposits are rocks and mineral ore deposits formed by the action of hydrothermal vents.
scenes.image_prompt: Hydrothermal fluids dispersing into the global ocean to create distinct plumes., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Geological conditions
scenes.line: Hydrothermal vents exist because the Earth is both geologically active and has large amounts of water on its surface and within its crust. Under the sea, they may form features called black smokers or white smokers, which deliver a wide range of elements to the world oceans.
scenes.image_prompt: Underwater geological activity with large amounts of water near the Earth crust., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Biological productivity
scenes.line: Relative to the majority of the deep sea, the areas around hydrothermal vents are biologically more productive. Chemosynthetic bacteria and archaea found around hydrothermal vents form the base of the food chain, supporting diverse organisms.
scenes.image_prompt: Biologically productive areas surrounding hydrothermal vents in the deep sea., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Diverse organisms
scenes.line: These support diverse organisms including giant tube worms, clams, limpets, and shrimp. Active hydrothermal vents are thought to exist on Jupiter moon Europa and Saturn moon Enceladus.
scenes.image_prompt: Giant tube worms, clams, limpets, and shrimp living near an active vent., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Ancient Mars
scenes.line: It is speculated that ancient hydrothermal vents once existed on Mars. Hydrothermal vents have been hypothesized to have been a significant factor to starting abiogenesis and the survival of primitive life.
scenes.image_prompt: Rocky and dusty landscape of the planet Mars under a pale sky., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Molecule synthesis
scenes.line: The conditions of these vents have been shown to support the synthesis of molecules important to life. Some evidence suggests that certain vents such as alkaline hydrothermal vents or those containing supercritical CO2 are more conducive to the formation of these organic molecules.
scenes.image_prompt: Microscopic view of chemical molecules forming in a mineral-rich environment., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Mid-ocean ridges
scenes.line: Hydrothermal vents in the deep ocean typically form along the mid-ocean ridges, such as the East Pacific Rise and the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. These are locations where two tectonic plates are diverging and new crust is being formed.
scenes.image_prompt: Rugged terrain of an underwater mid-ocean ridge system., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Seawater drawn in
scenes.line: The water that issues from seafloor hydrothermal vents consists mostly of seawater drawn into the hydrothermal system close to the volcanic edifice. This water includes some magmatic water released by the upwelling magma.
scenes.image_prompt: Seawater drawn into faults and porous sediments near a volcanic edifice., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Land systems
scenes.line: On land, the majority of water circulated within fumarole and geyser systems is meteoric water and ground water that has percolated down. Land systems also commonly contain some portion of metamorphic water, magmatic water, and sedimentary formational brine released by the magma.
scenes.image_prompt: Fumarole and geyser systems releasing steam on a rocky land surface., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Temperature range
scenes.line: Water emerges from these vents at temperatures ranging from 60 °C up to as high as 464 °C. Due to the high hydrostatic pressure at these depths, water may exist in either its liquid form or as a supercritical fluid at such temperatures.
scenes.image_prompt: Shimmering superheated water emerging from a rocky seafloor fissure., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Salinity effects
scenes.line: However, introducing salinity into the fluid raises the critical point to higher temperatures and pressures. The critical point of seawater is 407 °C and 298.5 bars, corresponding to a depth of ~2,960 m below sea level.
scenes.image_prompt: Crystals forming in saline water under high pressure conditions., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Phase separation
scenes.line: Furthermore, the salinity of vent fluids have been shown to vary widely due to phase separation in the crust. Thus, water emerging from the hottest parts of some hydrothermal vents can be a supercritical fluid, possessing physical properties between those of a gas and those of a liquid.
scenes.image_prompt: Phase separation occurring within porous crustal rocks., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Sister Peak
scenes.line: Sister Peak vents low salinity phase-separated, vapor-type fluids. Sustained venting was not found to be supercritical but a brief injection of 464 °C was well above supercritical conditions.
scenes.image_prompt: Hydrothermal field vent emitting vapor-type fluids into the water column., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Turtle Pits
scenes.line: A nearby site, Turtle Pits, was found to vent low salinity fluid at 407 °C, which is above the critical point of the fluid at that salinity. A vent site in the Cayman Trough named Beebe, which is the world's deepest known hydrothermal site at ~5,000 m below sea level, has shown sustained supercritical venting.
scenes.image_prompt: Underwater vent site with dark mineral chimneys and shimmering water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Significance unknown
scenes.line: Although supercritical conditions have been observed at several sites, it is not yet known what significance supercritical venting has in terms of hydrothermal circulation. The initial stages of a vent chimney begin with the deposition of the mineral anhydrite.
scenes.image_prompt: Scientific deep-sea submersible exploring an uncharted hydrothermal vent., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Growth rate
scenes.line: Vent growths on the order of 30 cm per day have been recorded. An April 2007 exploration of the deep-sea vents off the coast of Fiji found those vents to be a significant source of dissolved iron.
scenes.image_prompt: Growing mineral chimney structure rising from the seabed., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Cylindrical chimneys
scenes.line: Some hydrothermal vents form roughly cylindrical chimney structures from minerals that are dissolved in the vent fluid. When the superheated water contacts the near-freezing sea water, the minerals precipitate out to form particles which add to the height of the stacks.
scenes.image_prompt: Cylindrical chimney structures built from dissolved minerals., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Chimney heights
scenes.line: Some of these chimney structures can reach heights of 60 m. An example of such a towering vent was Godzilla, a structure on the Pacific Ocean deep seafloor near Oregon that rose to 40 m before it fell over in 1996.
scenes.image_prompt: Tall mineral chimney reaching upward into the deep ocean darkness., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Bathyal zone
scenes.line: A black smoker or deep-sea vent is a type of hydrothermal vent found on the seabed, typically in the bathyal zone. They appear as black, chimney-like structures that emit a cloud of black material.
scenes.image_prompt: Bathyal zone of the seabed with dark water and vent fields., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Sulfur-bearing minerals
scenes.line: Black smokers typically emit particles with high levels of sulfur-bearing minerals, or sulfides. Some black smokers along the Azores segment of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge are exceptionally metal-rich; for instance, hydrothermal fluids from the Rainbow Vent Field contain up to 24,000 μM of dissolved iron.
scenes.image_prompt: Sulfur-bearing mineral particles billowing from a black smoker vent., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Discovery date
scenes.line: Black smokers were first discovered in 1979 on the East Pacific Rise by scientists from Scripps Institution of Oceanography during the RISE Project. They were observed using the deep submergence vehicle ALVIN from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.
scenes.image_prompt: Historic deep-sea research equipment used during oceanographic expeditions., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Loki Castle
scenes.line: The most northerly black smokers are a cluster of five named Loki Castle, discovered in 2008 by scientists from the University of Bergen on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. White smoker vents emit lighter-hued minerals, such as those containing barium, calcium and silicon.
scenes.image_prompt: Cluster of black smokers located in a northern stability zone of the ridge., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Lower temperature plumes
scenes.line: These vents also tend to have lower-temperature plumes probably because they are generally distant from their heat source. White smokers correspond mostly to waning stages of such hydrothermal fields, as magmatic heat sources become progressively more distant from the source.
scenes.image_prompt: Gentle white plumes rising from a hydrothermal vent opening., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Plume evolution
scenes.line: The phase during which hydrothermal plumes rise through the water column is known as the buoyant plume phase. Eventually, the coupled effects of dilution and rising into progressively warmer overlying seawater will cause the hydrothermal plume to become neutrally buoyant at some height above the seafloor.
scenes.image_prompt: Buoyant hydrothermal plume rising vertically through the deep water column., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Helium tracers
scenes.line: The noble gas helium fits this criterion and is a particularly useful tracer of hydrothermal activity as venting releases elevated concentrations of helium-3. Although life is very sparse at these depths, black smokers are the centers of entire ecosystems.
scenes.image_prompt: Bubbles and dissolved gases dispersing outward in an ocean plume., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Chemosynthesis Process
scenes.line: Sunlight is nonexistent, so many organisms convert heat, methane, and sulfur into energy through chemosynthesis. More complex life forms, such as clams and tubeworms, feed on these organisms.
scenes.image_prompt: Deep sea microbes under laboratory magnification showing chemical reactions., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Depositing Minerals
scenes.line: The organisms at the base of the food chain also deposit minerals into the base of the black smoker. A species of phototrophic bacterium has been found living near a black smoker off the coast of Mexico.
scenes.image_prompt: Mineral deposits accumulating at the base of a deep-sea vent structure., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Depth and Sunlight
scenes.line: No sunlight penetrates that far into the waters at a depth of 2,500 m. The bacteria, part of the Chlorobiaceae family, use the faint glow from the black smoker for photosynthesis.
scenes.image_prompt: Pitch black ocean water illuminated by a research submersible light., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Exclusive Light Source
scenes.line: This is the first organism discovered in nature to exclusively use a light other than sunlight for photosynthesis. The Pompeii worm Alvinella pompejana, capable of withstanding temperatures up to 80 °C, was found in the 1980s.
scenes.image_prompt: Deep sea bacteria absorbing faint thermal radiation., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Scaly-Foot Gastropod
scenes.line: The scaly-foot gastropod was first found in 2001 during an expedition to the Indian Ocean's Kairei hydrothermal vent field. The latter uses iron sulfides for the structure of its dermal sclerites instead of calcium carbonate.
scenes.image_prompt: A unique sea snail with metallic scales resting on a dark rock., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Pressure Stabilization
scenes.line: The extreme pressure of 2,500 m of water is thought to play a role in stabilizing iron sulfide. This armor plating probably serves as a defense against the venomous radula of predatory snails.
scenes.image_prompt: Deep sea pressure gauge instruments mounted on a metal frame., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Oldest Life Evidence
scenes.line: In March 2017, researchers reported evidence of possibly the oldest forms of life on Earth. Putative fossilized microorganisms were discovered in hydrothermal vent precipitates in the Nuvvuagittuq Belt.
scenes.image_prompt: Rock samples from an ancient geological formation laid out on a table., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Ancient Timeline
scenes.line: They may have lived as early as 4.280 billion years ago, not long after the oceans formed. Hydrothermal vent ecosystems have enormous biomass and productivity, but this rests on symbiotic relationships.
scenes.image_prompt: An artistic representation of early Earth with forming oceans and volcanic activity., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Chemoautotrophic Symbionts
scenes.line: Deep-sea vent ecosystems differ due to symbiosis between macroinvertebrate hosts and chemoautotrophic microbial symbionts. The microbial life found at hydrothermal vents is chemosynthetic; they fix carbon by using energy from chemicals.
scenes.image_prompt: Microscopic view of symbiotic bacteria inside animal tissue cells., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Toxic Sulfide
scenes.line: However, sulfide is an extremely toxic substance to most life on Earth. For this reason, scientists were astounded when they first found hydrothermal vents teeming with life in 1977.
scenes.image_prompt: Bubbles rising from a sulfur-rich underwater vent opening., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Gills Endosymbiosis
scenes.line: What was discovered was the ubiquitous symbiosis of chemoautotrophs living in the vent animals' gills. The host provides the symbiont with chemicals required for chemosynthesis, such as carbon, sulfide, and oxygen.
scenes.image_prompt: Detailed scientific illustration of a clam gill structure., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Tubeworm Trophosome
scenes.line: Tubeworms have no mouth and no gut, but they do have a trophosome where their endosymbionts are found. They also have a bright red plume which they use to uptake compounds such as O, H2S, and CO2.
scenes.image_prompt: An anatomical cross-section view of a giant tubeworm interior., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Hemoglobin Protection
scenes.line: Tubeworms hemoglobin is capable of carrying oxygen without interference or inhibition from sulfide. In 2005, it was discovered that this is possible due to zinc ions that bind the hydrogen sulfide.
scenes.image_prompt: Molecular model of hemoglobin binding with gas molecules., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Mussels Thiosulfate
scenes.line: In order to circumvent the toxicity of sulfide, mussels first convert it to thiosulfate. Shrimp found at vents in the Mid-Atlantic Ridge were discovered in 1988 to carry episymbionts.
scenes.image_prompt: Deep sea mussels attached to a dark basalt rock surface., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Methanotrophs
scenes.line: While some symbionts reduce sulfur compounds, others are known as methanotrophs and reduce methane. Life at the deep-sea hydrothermal vents could continue for millennia if the sun were to suddenly disappear.
scenes.image_prompt: Methane bubbles escaping through sediment on the ocean floor., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Thermal Energy Flux
scenes.line: Thermal energy flux is a permanent agent and is hypothesized to have contributed to the evolution of the planet. Günter Wächtershäuser proposed the iron-sulfur world theory and suggested that life might have originated at vents.
scenes.image_prompt: Magma chambers glowing beneath the Earth's oceanic crust., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Prebiotic Chemistry
scenes.line: Amino acid synthesis could have occurred deep in the Earth's crust and shot up along with hydrothermal fluids. Surfaces of mineral particles inside hydrothermal vents have similar catalytic properties to enzymes.
scenes.image_prompt: Mineral-rich fluid jetting out of a rocky seafloor fissure., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Supercritical CO2
scenes.line: The discovery of supercritical CO2 at some sites has been used to further support the theory of hydrothermal origin. Supercritical CO2 acts as a solvent that facilitates an environment conducive to dehydration synthesis.
scenes.image_prompt: Fluid in a supercritical state swirling inside a high-pressure chamber., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Alkaline Vents
scenes.line: There is some evidence that links the origin of life to alkaline hydrothermal vents in particular. The naturally occurring proton gradients at these deep sea vents supplemented the lack of phospholipid membranes.
scenes.image_prompt: White mineral formations of an alkaline hydrothermal vent field., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Nick Lane Argument
scenes.line: Nick Lane argues that the counterpoint largely misinterprets both his work and the work of others. An article in Science journal used data from experiments at the Lost City hydrothermal field.
scenes.image_prompt: A researcher reviewing notes and scientific papers at a desk., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Red Sea Brines
scenes.line: In 1949, a deep water survey reported anomalously hot brines in the central portion of the Red Sea. The hot solutions were emanating from an active subseafloor rift.
scenes.image_prompt: Shimmering dense brine pool resting on the deep sea floor., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Galapagos Rift
scenes.line: In June 1976, scientists obtained the first evidence for submarine hydrothermal vents along the Galápagos Rift. Transponders were deployed at the site, which was nicknamed Clam-bake, to enable an expedition to return.
scenes.image_prompt: A deep-towed camera sled suspended above the Pacific ocean floor., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Direct Observation
scenes.line: Ecosystems surrounding the Galápagos Rift vents were first directly observed in 1977. Corliss and van Andel observed and sampled the vents and their ecosystem on February 17, 1977.
scenes.image_prompt: The research submersible Alvin descending into the deep blue ocean., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: RISE Expedition
scenes.line: The RISE expedition explored the East Pacific Rise at 21° N in spring 1979. On Easter Sunday April 15, 1979 during a dive of Alvin to 2,600 meters, a vent field was found.
scenes.image_prompt: A research ship sailing across open ocean waters during an expedition., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Black Mineral Jets
scenes.line: On April 21, William Normark and Thierry Juteau discovered high temperature vents emitting black mineral jets. Macdonald and Jim Aiken rigged a temperature probe to Alvin to measure the water temperature.
scenes.image_prompt: Dark mineral smoke billowing from a towering chimney structure., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Highest Temperatures
scenes.line: This observed the highest temperatures then recorded at deep sea hydrothermal vents at 380±30 °C. In 2005, a mineral exploration company named Neptune Resources NL applied for and was granted 35,000 km2 of exploration rights.
scenes.image_prompt: Heat shimmer distorting the water around a glowing hydrothermal vent tip., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Kermadec Arc
scenes.line: These exploration rights were over the Kermadec Arc located in New Zealand's Exclusive Economic Zone. The company aimed to explore for seafloor massive sulfide deposits formed from modern hydrothermal vent fields.
scenes.image_prompt: Rugged volcanic islands rising steeply from deep ocean waters., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Medusa Vent Field
scenes.line: The discovery of the Medusa hydrothermal vent field in the Pacific Ocean offshore of Costa Rica was announced in April 2007. The Ashadze hydrothermal field at 13°N on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge had an elevation of -4200 m.
scenes.image_prompt: Deep blue ocean surface with distant tropical coastline., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Mid-Cayman Rise
scenes.line: This site is located on the 110 km long, ultraslow spreading Mid-Cayman Rise within the Cayman Trough. In early 2013, the deepest known hydrothermal vents were discovered in the Caribbean Sea at a depth of almost 5,000 metres.
scenes.image_prompt: An underwater canyon with steep rocky walls under heavy pressure., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Juan de Fuca
scenes.line: Oceanographers are studying the volcanoes and hydrothermal vents of the Juan de Fuca mid ocean ridge where tectonic plates move apart. Hydrothermal vents and other geothermal manifestations are currently being explored in the Bahía de Concepción, Baja California Sur, Mexico.
scenes.image_prompt: A computer visualization of colliding tectonic plates beneath the ocean floor., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Active Vent Fields
scenes.line: As of 2009 there were approximately 500 known active submarine hydrothermal vent fields distributed along plate boundaries. Researchers recognized at least 11 biogeographic provinces of hydrothermal vent systems across the global ocean basins.
scenes.image_prompt: A glowing scientific globe showing underwater seismic fault lines., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Mount Isa Orebody
scenes.line: The Mount Isa orebody located in Queensland, Australia, is an example of seafloor massive sulfide deposits forming exploitable mineral resources. Many hydrothermal vents are rich in cobalt, gold, copper, and rare earth metals essential for electronic components.
scenes.image_prompt: An open-cut mining landscape with tiered earth terraces., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Iron Formations
scenes.line: Hydrothermal venting on the Archean seafloor is considered to have formed Algoma-type banded iron formations as a source of iron ore. Mineral exploration companies turned their attention to the extraction of mineral resources from seafloor hydrothermal fields.
scenes.image_prompt: A slab of layered sedimentary rock showing red and grey bands., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Japanese Imports
scenes.line: In countries such as Japan, where mineral resources are primarily derived from imports, there is a push for seafloor extraction. The world's first large-scale mining of vent mineral deposits was carried out by JOGMEC in August and September 2017.
scenes.image_prompt: A cargo container ship docked at an industrial seaport., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Okinawa Trough
scenes.line: This mining occurred at the Izena cauldron vent field within the Okinawa Trough containing 15 confirmed vent fields. Nautilus Minerals is in advanced stages of commencing extraction from its Solwarra deposit in the Bismarck Archipelago.
scenes.image_prompt: A calm sea surface under a bright overcast sky., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Modified Technology
scenes.line: Both companies are proposing using modified existing technology for their deep sea mining operations. Nautilus Minerals succeeded in returning over 10 metric tons of mined SMS using modified drum cutters mounted on an ROV.
scenes.image_prompt: Engineers working on mechanical drill parts in a workshop., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Suction Pump
scenes.line: Neptune Minerals succeeded in recovering SMS sediment samples using a modified oil industry suction pump mounted on an ROV. Potential seafloor mining impacts include dust plumes, collapsing vents, methane clathrate release, and sub-oceanic landslides.
scenes.image_prompt: A large industrial vacuum hose coiled on a factory floor., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Noise Pollution
scenes.line: Submerged mining tools and surface support vessels inevitably create noise pollution in the deep ocean. Vent organisms experience very little sound and have evolved highly sensitive hearing organs vulnerable to sudden noise increases.

Their mission was a two-part program surveying three hydrothermal vent sites in the southern Mariana Trough backarc basin using the autonomous underwater vehicle Urashima.

scenes.label: Ashura Lander
scenes.line: The second goal of the cruise was to deploy a new 10K free fall camera system called Ashura to sample sediments and biologics at the bottom. The lander Ashura made two descents, bottoming on the first on 6 July 2009 at 10,867 metres.
scenes.image_prompt: Metal deep-sea lander frame outfitted with spherical flotation and camera gear, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Second Descent
scenes.line: The second descent on 10 July 2009 reached 10,897 metres with the 270 kg Ashura equipped with multiple baited traps. On 7 October 2010, further sonar mapping was conducted by the US Center for Coastal and Ocean Mapping aboard the 4,762-ton Sumner.
scenes.image_prompt: Underwater metal trap cage fitted with bait containers, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Preliminary Determination
scenes.line: The CCOM/JHC team preliminary determined that the Challenger Deep has a maximum depth of 10,994 m. A secondary deep with a depth of 10,951 m was located at approximately 23.75 nmi to the east in the eastern basin.
scenes.image_prompt: Hydrographic map showing high-resolution ocean trench bathymetry data, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Joint Expedition
scenes.line: JAMSTEC returned Yokosuka to the Challenger Deep with cruise YK10-16 from 21 to 28 November 2010 under chief scientist Hiroshi Kitazato. The Danish Ultra Deep Lander System was employed by Ronnie Glud et al. on four casts.
scenes.image_prompt: Researchers in safety vests working on the aft deck of a research vessel, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Deepest Record
scenes.line: The deepest depth recorded was on 28 November 2010 during camera cast CS5 at a corrected depth of 10,889.6 metres. With JAMSTEC Cruises YK13-09 and YK13-12, Yokosuka hosted chief scientist Hidetaka Nomaki for a trip to obtain DNA/RNA on large amphipods.
scenes.image_prompt: Digital depth readout screen displaying numerical ocean measurements, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Benthic Lander
scenes.line: Hideki Kobayashi and the team deployed a benthic lander on 23 November 2013 with eleven baited traps into the central basin. After an eight-hour, 46-minute stay at the bottom, they recovered some 90 individual Hirondellea gigas.
scenes.image_prompt: Deep-sea benthic lander apparatus resting on a vessel preparation dock, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Kairei Expedition
scenes.line: JAMSTEC deployed Kairei to the Challenger Deep again 11–17 January 2014, under the leadership of chief scientist Takuro Nunora. The 11,000-meter capable crawler-driven ROV ABISMO was sent to 7,646 m depth to identify possible hydrothermal activity.
scenes.image_prompt: Japanese research ship underway on the open sea, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Falkor Deployment
scenes.line: From 16 to 19 December 2014, the Schmidt Ocean Institute vessel Falkor deployed four different untethered instruments. Both Deep Sound probes recorded acoustics floating at 9,000 metres depth until Deep Sound 3 imploded at 8,620 metres.
scenes.image_prompt: Modern oceanographic research vessel with A-frame crane on stern, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Leggo Photography
scenes.line: Leggo landed at an uncorrected depth of 11,168 metres and returned with good photography of amphipods feeding on mackerel bait. From 10 to 13 July 2015, the US Coast Guard Cutter Sequoia hosted researchers in deploying a Full-Ocean Depth Mooring.
scenes.image_prompt: Underwater camera housing mounted on a heavy metal frame, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Hydrophone Array
scenes.line: A 6-hour descent into the western basin anchored the 45-meter-long moored deep-ocean hydrophone and pressure sensor array. Observed sound sources included earthquake signals, cetacean vocalizations, ship propeller sounds, airguns, active sonar, and a typhoon.
scenes.image_prompt: Cylindrical hydrophone acoustic recording instrument being prepared for deployment, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Xiangyanghong Cruise
scenes.line: The research vessel Xiangyanghong 09 deployed on Leg II of the 37th China Cruise Dayang to the Challenger Deep western basin. As the mother ship for China's manned deep submersible Jiaolong, the expedition carried out an exploration of the hadal zone.
scenes.image_prompt: Large red and white research vessel at sea under overcast skies, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Tansuo 1 Voyage
scenes.line: From 22 June to 12 August 2016, the Chinese submersible support ship Tansuo 1 deployed to the Challenger Deep on her maiden voyage. On 12 July 2016, the ROV Haidou-1 dived to a depth of 10,767 metres in the Challenger Deep area.
scenes.image_prompt: Large marine support vessel with specialized heavy lifting cranes, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Sonne Mapping
scenes.line: In November 2016 sonar mapping was conducted aboard the 8,554-ton Deep Ocean Research Vessel Sonne. The team determined that the Challenger Deep has a maximum depth of 10,925 m at 11°19.945′N 142°12.123′E.
scenes.image_prompt: Large ocean research vessel navigating through open blue waters, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Velocity Profiles
scenes.line: The observed depth discrepancy with earlier surveys are related to the application of differing sound velocity profiles. In December 2016, the research vessel Shiyan 3 deployed 33 broadband seismometers onto both the backarc and the southern Pacific Plate.
scenes.image_prompt: Scientific graph illustrating ocean temperature and sound velocity profiles, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Zhang Jian Departure
scenes.line: The newly launched research vessel Zhang Jian departed Shanghai on 3 December to test three new deep-sea landers. From 25 to 27 December, three deep-sea landing devices descended into the trench, with the third device bringing back 103 amphipods.
scenes.image_prompt: Newly built scientific research vessel moored at a harbor dock, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Tansuo-1 Return
scenes.line: Tansuo-1 returned to the Challenger Deep 20 January – 5 February 2017 with baited traps for macrobiology. On 29 January they recovered photography and samples of a new species of snailfish designated Pseudoliparis swirei.
scenes.image_prompt: Oceanographic research ship working on calm tropical seas, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Shinyo Maru Expedition
scenes.line: Tokyo University dispatched the research vessel Shinyo Maru to the Mariana Trench with baited traps on 20 January 2017. Water samples were collected at Challenger Deep from 11 layers of the Mariana Trench in March 2017 using Niskin bottles.
scenes.image_prompt: University research vessel sailing near coastal island waters, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: UROV11K Testing
scenes.line: JAMSTEC deployed Kairei in May 2017 for the express purpose of testing the new full-ocean depth ROV UROV11K. On UROV11K's ascent from 10,899 metres on 14 May 2017, the ROV's buoyancy failed at 5,320 metres depth.
scenes.image_prompt: Remotely operated vehicle outfitted with bright yellow flotation modules, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Compact Lander
scenes.line: Murashima directed the Kairei to test a new Compact Hadal Lander which made three descents for photography. The twin-hulled scientific research vessel Shen Kuo departed Shanghai on 25 November 2018 and returned on 8 January 2019.
scenes.image_prompt: Compact tripod lander structure equipped with underwater cameras, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Navigation Trial
scenes.line: On 13 December they tested a system of underwater navigation at a depth exceeding 10,000 metres during a field trial. Project leader Tsui Veichen stated that with the Tsaihungyuy equipment at depth it was possible to obtain a signal and determine exact geolocations.
scenes.image_prompt: Acoustic transducer and underwater communication hardware on a workbench, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Kaiko Recovery
scenes.line: On the morning of 17 October, ROV Kaikō dive #272 began and was recovered over 33 hours later. Traps brought up large numbers of amphipods and cameras recorded holothurians, white polychaetes, tube worms, and other species.
scenes.image_prompt: Heavy robotic tethered vehicle hanging from a ship gantry crane, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: GPS Accuracy
scenes.line: During its 2002 survey, Kairei had access to non-degraded GPS positional services and achieved single-digit meter accuracy. The 2002 surveys of both basins were tight, with meticulous cross-gridding of the eastern basin with ten parallel tracks.
scenes.image_prompt: Global positioning satellite antenna dome mounted on a ship mast, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

long_what_sank_rms_titanic_on_her_maiden.title: What Sank RMS Titanic on Her Maiden Voyage?

scenes.label: Deadliest Peacetime Sinking
scenes.line: RMS Titanic was a British ocean liner that sank in the early hours of 15 April 1912 after striking an iceberg on her maiden voyage from Southampton, England, to New York City. Of the 2,208 passengers and crew aboard, approximately 1,500 died, making the incident one of the deadliest peacetime sinkings of a single ship.
scenes.image_prompt: An ocean liner at sea under a clear sky., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: White Star Line
scenes.line: Titanic was operated by the White Star Line, one of the premier transatlantic services, and carried some of the wealthiest people in the world, as well as hundreds of emigrants. The disaster drew public attention, spurred major changes in maritime safety regulations, and inspired a lasting legacy in popular culture.
scenes.image_prompt: A large passenger ship docked at a port terminal., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Olympic Class
scenes.line: At the time of her voyage, she was the largest ship afloat upon entering service and the second of three Olympic-class ocean liners built for the White Star Line. The ship was built by the Harland and Wolff shipbuilding company in Belfast and had advanced safety features, such as watertight compartments and remotely activated watertight doors.
scenes.image_prompt: Ship hull under construction in a large shipyard., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: The Unsinkable Ship
scenes.line: These advanced safety features contributed to the ship's reputation as unsinkable. Additionally, the ship was equipped with twenty lifeboats: fourteen regular lifeboats, two emergency cutters, and four collapsible boats.
scenes.image_prompt: Steel bulkhead doors inside a ship compartment., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Successful Launches
scenes.line: Of the twenty boats, eighteen were launched successfully. The first-class accommodations were designed to be the pinnacle of comfort and luxury.
scenes.image_prompt: Ropes and davits on the deck of a vintage ship., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Onboard Amenities
scenes.line: They included a gymnasium, swimming pool, smoking rooms, fine restaurants and cafes, a Victorian-style Turkish bath, and opulent cabins. A high-powered spark-gap transmitter was provided by the Marconi Marine Company for first-class passenger use.
scenes.image_prompt: Indoor swimming pool with tiled walls and pillars., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Immigration Focus
scenes.line: However, the ship was primarily built as an immigration ship designed to carry around 1,000 third-class passengers. It provided comfortable accommodations for the standards of the time, including a dining saloon and an open space free for their personal use.
scenes.image_prompt: Empty wooden dining benches inside a large hall., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Mythological Origin
scenes.line: The name Titanic derives from the Titans of Greek mythology. Built in Belfast, Ireland, RMS Titanic was the second of the three Olympic-class ocean liners—the lead vessel was RMS Olympic and the final ship in the class would be RMS Britannic.
scenes.image_prompt: Carved stone classical statues in an exhibition hall., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: White Star Fleet
scenes.line: They were by far the largest vessels of the British shipping company White Star Line's fleet, which comprised 29 steamers and tenders by 1912. White Star faced an increasing challenge from its main rivals, Cunard Line, and the German lines Hamburg America and Norddeutscher Lloyd.
scenes.image_prompt: Vintage steamships anchored in a busy harbor., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Size Over Speed
scenes.line: Ismay preferred to compete on size rather than speed and proposed to commission a new class of liners larger than anything that had come before. The new ships would have sufficient speed to maintain a weekly service with only three ships instead of the original four.
scenes.image_prompt: Architectural blueprints spread out on a wooden drafting table., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Replacement Liners
scenes.line: Olympic and Titanic would replace RMS Teutonic of 1889, RMS Majestic of 1890 and RMS Adriatic of 1907. RMS Oceanic first departed from a new home port in June 1907 along with the Teutonic, Majestic, and the new Adriatic on the Southampton-New York run.
scenes.image_prompt: Vintage passenger steamer underway on the water., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Long Relationship
scenes.line: The ships were constructed by the Belfast shipbuilder Harland & Wolff, which had a long-established relationship with the White Star Line dating back to 1867. Harland and Wolff were given a great deal of latitude in designing ships for the White Star Line.
scenes.image_prompt: Industrial brick buildings of a historic shipyard., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Cost Considerations
scenes.line: Cost considerations were a relatively low priority; Harland & Wolff were authorised to spend what it needed on the ships, plus a five per cent profit margin. In the case of the Olympic-class ships, a cost of £3 million for the first two ships was agreed, plus extras to contract and the usual five per cent fee.
scenes.image_prompt: Ledger book with handwritten financial entries., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Design Leadership
scenes.line: Harland and Wolff put their leading designers to work designing Olympic-class vessels under the oversight of Lord Pirrie and Thomas Andrews. The team included Edward Wilding, responsible for calculating the ship's design, stability and trim, and Alexander Carlisle, the shipyard's chief draughtsman.
scenes.image_prompt: Men in formal suits studying engineering drawings., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Hull Numbers
scenes.line: At this point, the first ship had no name but was referred to simply as Number 400, and Titanic was based on a revised version and given the number 401. Titanic was 882 feet 9 inches long with a maximum breadth of 92 feet 6 inches.
scenes.image_prompt: Metal plaque bearing an industrial hull number., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Height and Tonnage
scenes.line: The ship's total height, measured from the base of the keel to the top of the bridge, was 104 feet. Titanic measured 46,329 GRT and 21,831 NRT and with a draught of 34 feet 7 inches and displaced 52,310 tonnes.
scenes.image_prompt: Tall ship mast viewed from the base looking upward., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Ten Decks
scenes.line: All three of the Olympic-class ships had ten decks, excluding the top of the officers' quarters, eight of which were for passenger use. The boat deck housed the lifeboats, the bridge, the wheelhouse, and the First Class Grand Staircase entrance.
scenes.image_prompt: Stacked levels of wooden decks on a passenger ship., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Promenades
scenes.line: The wood-covered deck was divided into four segregated promenades for officers, First Class passengers, engineers, and Second Class passengers respectively. A Deck, also called the promenade deck, extended along the entire 546 feet length of the superstructure and was reserved exclusively for First Class passengers.
scenes.image_prompt: Long wooden deck corridor with chairs along the wall., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: B Deck Staterooms
scenes.line: B Deck, the bridge deck, was the top weight-bearing deck and the uppermost level of the hull, featuring six palatial staterooms with private promenades. On Titanic, the à la carte restaurant and the Café Parisien provided luxury dining facilities to First Class passengers.
scenes.image_prompt: Luxury cabin interior with upholstered armchairs., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Forecastle and Poop
scenes.line: The raised forecastle of the ship was forward of the bridge deck, while aft of the bridge deck was the raised poop deck, 106 feet long. C Deck, the shelter deck, was the highest deck to run uninterrupted from stem to stern.
scenes.image_prompt: Forward bow section of a large ship with machinery., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: D Deck Public Rooms
scenes.line: D Deck, the saloon deck, was dominated by three public rooms—the First-Class reception room, the First-Class dining saloon and the Second-Class dining saloon. Along the length of E Deck ran a long passageway nicknamed Scotland Road, used by Third Class passengers and crew members.
scenes.image_prompt: Large dining hall with high ceilings and pillars., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: F Deck Facilities
scenes.line: The Third Class dining saloon was located on F Deck, as was the First Class bath complex, containing the swimming pool and the Turkish bath. The first-class squash court was located on G Deck along with the travelling post office where letters and parcels were sorted ready for delivery.
scenes.image_prompt: Tiled steam room doorway in a bath facility., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Engine Rooms
scenes.line: The tank top provided the platform on which the ship's boilers, engines, turbines and electrical generators were housed. Titanic propulsion was supplied by three main engines—two reciprocating four-cylinder, triple-expansion steam engines and one centrally placed low-pressure Parsons turbine.
scenes.image_prompt: Massive steel piston rods inside an engine room., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Combined Power
scenes.line: The two reciprocating engines had a combined output of 30,000 horsepower, and the output of the steam turbine was 16,000 horsepower. The engines were powered by steam produced in 29 boilers, 24 of which were double-ended and five single-ended, which contained a total of 159 furnaces.
scenes.image_prompt: Pressure gauges mounted on a metal wall panel., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Stoking Coal
scenes.line: The furnaces required over 600 tonnes of coal a day to be shovelled into them by hand, requiring the services of 176 firemen working around the clock. There were three propellers; the outer wing propellers were the largest, each carrying three blades of manganese-bronze alloy.
scenes.image_prompt: Metal coal shovel resting on a brick floor., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Electrical Plant
scenes.line: Titanic's electrical plant was capable of producing more power than an average city power station of the time. Titanic's radiotelegraph equipment was provided by the Marconi International Marine Communication Company, which supplied wireless operators Jack Phillips and Harold Bride.
scenes.image_prompt: Electrical control switchboards with analog dials., cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Steerage Accommodations
scenes.line: Third Class accommodations aboard Titanic were not as luxurious as First or Second Class but were better than on many other ships of the time. The established arrangement was that single men were quartered in the forward areas, while single women, married couples and families were quartered aft.
scenes.image_prompt: An empty wooden ship cabin with bunk beds, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Cabin Amenities
scenes.line: White Star Line vessels provided their Third-Class passengers with private, small but comfortable cabins capable of accommodating two, four, six, eight and ten passengers. Third Class accommodations also included their own dining rooms, as well as public gathering areas including adequate open deck space.
scenes.image_prompt: A simple narrow bunk bed inside a rustic cabin room, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Leisure Facilities
scenes.line: As well as making use of the indoor amenities such as the library, smoking rooms, and gymnasium, it was also customary for passengers to socialise on the open deck. A passenger list was published before the sailing to inform the public which members of the great and good were on board.
scenes.image_prompt: People relaxing on wooden benches on a ship deck, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Grand Staircase Design
scenes.line: One of Titanic's most distinctive features was the First Class staircase, known as the Grand Staircase or Grand Stairway. Built of solid English oak with a sweeping curve, the staircase descended through seven decks of the ship, between the boat deck to E deck.
scenes.image_prompt: A wide wooden staircase curving upward inside a large hall, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Natural Light
scenes.line: It was capped with a dome of wrought iron and glass that admitted natural light to the stairwell. At the uppermost landing was a large carved wooden panel containing a clock, with figures of Honour and Glory Crowning Time flanking the clock face.
scenes.image_prompt: A glass and iron dome ceiling structure inside a building, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Exploration Void
scenes.line: The Grand Staircase was destroyed during the sinking and is now just a void in the ship which modern explorers have used to access the lower decks. For the storage of letters, parcels and specie, 26,800 cubic feet of space was allocated.
scenes.image_prompt: Dark underwater metal framing seen through a narrow opening, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Sea Post Office
scenes.line: The Sea Post Office on G Deck was manned by five postal clerks who worked 13 hours a day, sorting up to 60,000 items daily. Another 19,455 cubic feet was taken up by first- and second-class baggage.
scenes.image_prompt: Postal letters and parcels scattered across sorting tables, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Standard Cargo
scenes.line: In addition, there was a considerable quantity of regular cargo, ranging from furniture to foodstuffs, and a 1912 Renault Type CE Coupe de Ville motor car. Titanic was equipped with eight electric cranes, four electric winches and three steam winches to lift cargo and baggage in and out of the holds.
scenes.image_prompt: A vintage classic automobile parked inside a factory floor, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Lifeboat Inventory
scenes.line: Like Olympic, Titanic carried a total of 20 lifeboats: 14 standard wooden Harland and Wolff lifeboats and four Engelhardt collapsible lifeboats. All of the lifeboats were stowed securely on the boat deck and, except for collapsible lifeboats A and B, connected to davits by ropes.
scenes.image_prompt: A row of wooden lifeboats mounted on a ship deck, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Davits Capacity
scenes.line: Titanic had 16 sets of Welin davits, each able to handle three lifeboats. At the time, the Board of Trade's regulations required British vessels over 10,000 tonnes to carry only 16 lifeboats with a capacity of 990 occupants.
scenes.image_prompt: A row of iron davit arms mounted along a ship rail, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Shipyard Construction
scenes.line: The ships were constructed on Queen's Island, now known as the Titanic Quarter, in Belfast Harbour. The Arrol Gantry stood 228 feet high, was 270 feet wide and 840 feet long and weighed more than 6,000 tonnes.
scenes.image_prompt: Large industrial shipyard cranes towering over a waterfront, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Double Bottom
scenes.line: At the base of the ships, a double bottom 5 feet 3 inches deep supported 300 frames, each between 24 and 36 inches apart. The 2,000 hull plates were single pieces of rolled steel plate, mostly up to 6 feet wide and 30 feet long.
scenes.image_prompt: Ribbed metal frames forming the bottom skeleton of a ship hull, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Rivets Used
scenes.line: Like most other iron and steel structures of the era, the hull was held together with over three million iron and steel rivets. Twenty Clydesdale draught horses were needed to haul the centre anchor by wagon from the Noah Hingley & Sons Ltd forge shop.
scenes.image_prompt: Thousands of small metal rivets spilled onto a metal workbench, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Construction Hazards
scenes.line: 246 injuries were recorded during Titanic's construction, including 28 severe injuries, such as arms severed by machines or legs crushed. Titanic was launched at 12:15 pm on 31 May 1911 in the presence of Lord Pirrie, J. Pierpont Morgan, J. Bruce Ismay and 100,000 onlookers.
scenes.image_prompt: Industrial machinery inside a heavy metal workshop, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Soap Lubrication
scenes.line: Twenty-two tonnes of soap and tallow were spread on the slipway to lubricate the ship's passage into the River Lagan. The most noticeable exterior difference was that Titanic had a steel screen with sliding windows installed along the forward half of the A Deck promenade.
scenes.image_prompt: Thick white soap smeared across large wooden planks on a slipway, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Dry Dock Entry
scenes.line: On 3 February 1912, Titanic was pulled into Thompson Graving Dock. Titanic's sea trials began at 6 am on Tuesday, 2 April 1912, two days after the fitting out was finished.
scenes.image_prompt: A massive stone dry dock with concrete walls and empty floor, cinematic deep sea photography, dramatic underwater lighting, bioluminescent glow, hyper-realistic, 8k resolution, National Geographic style

scenes.label: Trial Speed
scenes.line: Titanic covered a distance of about 80 nautical miles, averaging 18 knots and reaching a maximum speed of just under 21 knots. On returning to Belfast at about 7 pm, the surveyor signed an Agreement and Account of Voyages and Crew, valid for 12 months.
